entries.postTitle: How to Cancel AI Advantage Current Refund and Subscription Terms

captions.threads:
i've been through enough subscription cancellations to know that "simple" and "billing" don't belong in the same sentence. you think you're covered, you think the guarantee means something, then you hit the fine print and realize your timeline was three weeks ago.

1/4 the trap isn't malice. it's usually just that every offer, every product tier, every seasonal campaign has its own rules living in different documents. your refund window might be 30 days. might be 14. might reset based on when you actually access the thing versus when you paid for it. nobody tells you this until you need it.

2/4 what actually matters: knowing your specific terms before you need them. not the general "refund policy" page. the terms attached to the thing you bought. screenshot them. put them in a note. this sounds paranoid until it saves you from arguing with support in week five when you realize you're out of time.

3/4 the cancellation itself is usually straightforward once you know what you're looking for. the hard part is that knowledge lives scattered, and companies count on you not having it. they're not trying to trap you. they're just not trying to make this obvious either.

4/4 clarity about your own agreements is a form of self-respect. you're not being difficult by knowing when your window closes or what gets refunded. you're being awake. that matters more than the cancellation itself.

entries.postTitle: Automation vs Batch Creation for Artists

captions.threads:
1/4 I set up a Zapier automation last year that was supposed to handle my content scheduling. Three months later I was getting digest emails I never read, watching posts go out at times nobody I know was actually online, and feeling this weird distance from work that used to feel alive. That's when I realized automation and batch creation are solving different problems wearing the same name.

2/4 Automation wants to remove you from the loop. It's beautiful for things that genuinely don't need your presence, your intuition, your moment-to-moment awareness. But content? Your voice lives in the friction of creation. When you batch create, you're building momentum, finding patterns in your own thinking, staying close enough to course-correct. You're still in conversation with the work.

3/4 The trick isn't choosing one. It's being honest about which parts of your process actually benefit from being hands-off versus which parts need your attention. Maybe you automate your email lists but batch your creative output. Maybe you set up distribution workflows but keep ideation live. The specificity matters more than the ideology.

4/4 What I found is that creators who thrive aren't the ones with the most sophisticated automation. They're the ones who stayed connected to why they make things in the first place. The tools should fade. Your voice shouldn't.

Sit with this one.
